label: The two-sample t statistic: t equals the difference between the two sample means, x bar one minus x bar two, divided by the pooled standard error — s pooled times the square root of one over n one plus one over n two — where s pooled is the square root of the pooled variance; under the null hypothesis this follows Student's t distribution with n one plus n two minus two degrees of freedom

The pooled variance: s pooled squared equals the two sample variances weighted by their degrees of freedom — (n one minus one) times s one squared plus (n two minus one) times s two squared — divided by the total degrees of freedom, n one plus n two minus two

The Welch t statistic: the difference in means divided by a standard error built from each group's own variance — the square root of s one squared over n one plus s two squared over n two — with degrees of freedom from the Welch–Satterthwaite equation

The paired t statistic: t equals the mean of the n within-pair differences, d bar, divided by its standard error, the standard deviation of the differences over the square root of n, with n minus one degrees of freedom — the common level of each pair cancels, so each subject serves as their own control

The confidence interval for a mean difference: the estimate (difference in means, or mean of the differences) plus or minus the two-sided t critical value for the relevant degrees of freedom, t sub 1 minus alpha over 2, times the standard error — for a two-sided 5% test the critical value is t sub 0.975

Cohen's d: the standardized mean difference, the difference between the two means divided by the pooled standard deviation — a unit-free effect size, interpreted by the common convention 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (rules of thumb, not laws)
